subjects.name: Pharmacokinetics
defs: Movement of a drug from its administration site through body membranes into the bloodstream.
Circulation at the absorption site that carries absorbed drug into systemic circulation.
Special layers on oral preparations that modify the rate of drug absorption.
The physical preparation of a drug that affects how quickly it is absorbed.
Metabolism of an oral drug in the liver before it enters systemic circulation.
Influence of food in the gut on the absorption of oral medications.
Movement of stomach contents that can speed or slow drug absorption.
Ability of a drug to dissolve in lipids, speeding absorption across membranes.
Size of drug molecules, with smaller molecules absorbed more readily than large ones.
The path by which a medication enters the body and becomes available for absorption.
Gastric pH that can alter the absorption of orally administered drugs.
Extent of absorbing membrane, with larger areas allowing faster drug absorption.
Plasma protein that binds many drugs and influences their distribution.
Protective system that limits entry of many drugs into the central nervous system.
Ease with which a drug crosses cell membranes to reach target tissues.
Movement of a drug through the body after it has been absorbed.
Unbound portion of a drug able to cross membranes and produce effects.
Drug that crosses membranes readily and distributes widely throughout tissues.
Attachment of drugs to plasma proteins that limits free drug available to tissues.
Blood flow delivering drug to tissues, affecting concentration at target sites.
Apparent body volume into which a drug disperses after entering circulation.
Drug that crosses membranes poorly and distributes less widely than lipid-soluble drugs.
Product of drug metabolism that retains pharmacologic activity in the body.
Chronic liver disease that reduces drug metabolism and raises toxicity risk.
Family of liver enzymes that metabolize many lipid-soluble drugs.
Process by which enzymes reduce or eliminate toxic effects of drugs.
Increase in metabolic enzyme activity that accelerates drug breakdown.
Decrease in metabolic enzyme activity that slows drug breakdown.
Metabolism of drugs that occurs primarily in the liver by specialized enzymes.
Product of drug metabolism that lacks pharmacologic activity and is excreted.
Blood markers such as AST and ALT used to assess hepatic function.
Chemical conversion of a drug into forms that can be more readily eliminated.
Elimination of drugs or metabolites through bile into the feces.
Measure of kidney filtration rate used to assess drug elimination capacity.
Elimination of drugs and their metabolites from the body.
Elimination of drug metabolites from the body through the stool.
Kidney process that filters water-soluble drugs into urine for elimination.
Elimination of volatile drugs through the lungs during respiration.
Elimination of drugs and metabolites primarily through the kidneys and urine.
Reduced kidney function that decreases drug excretion and increases toxicity risk.
Acidity of urine that can alter renal elimination of certain drugs.
Fraction of an administered dose that reaches systemic circulation unchanged.
Volume of blood cleared of drug per unit time by elimination processes.
Build-up of drug in the body when dosing exceeds elimination.
Length of time a drug produces a therapeutic response.
Time required for serum drug concentration to decrease by one half.
Lowest drug concentration that produces a therapeutic response.
Time required for a drug to produce its first therapeutic response.
Time required for a drug to reach its maximum therapeutic response.
Equilibrium where drug administration rate equals elimination rate.
Range of doses that are both safe and effective for a drug.
Range of drug concentrations producing benefit without causing toxicity.

subjects.name: Pharmacodynamics
defs: Strength of binding between a drug and its receptor.
A signaling molecule produced inside the body that binds a receptor.
A protein target that many drugs inhibit to alter cellular function.
A substance from outside the body, such as a drug, that binds a receptor.
A membrane gate that opens or closes to allow ions or drugs to pass.
Any molecule that binds to a receptor to produce or block a response.
A protein on or in a cell that binds a specific messenger and triggers a response.
A variant form of a receptor with distinct tissue distribution or drug sensitivity.
An intracellular signaling molecule activated after a drug binds its receptor.
Preference of a drug for binding one receptor type over others.
The intracellular process that converts receptor binding into a cellular response.
A drug that binds a receptor and activates it to produce a biological effect.
A drug that binds a receptor at a site other than the active site.
A drug that binds a receptor without activating it, blocking other molecules.
An antagonist that reversibly competes with an agonist for the same receptor site.
The temporary binding of a drug to its receptor that initiates a response.
An agonist that produces the maximal possible receptor response.
An antagonist that binds covalently and permanently deactivates its receptor.
A drug that activates one receptor type while blocking another.
An antagonist that binds a different site and prevents maximal receptor response.
An agonist that activates a receptor but produces a weaker effect than a full agonist.
Drug-receptor attachment that can dissociate depending on affinity.
The maximal response a drug can produce regardless of further dose increases.
A graph relating drug concentration to the magnitude of biological response.
The concentration producing half of a drug's maximal response.
The dose producing the intended effect in half of a population.
The maximum effect a drug can produce at a tolerable dose.
The greatest response a drug can achieve on its dose-response curve.
A continuous increase in response as drug dose increases in one subject.
The dose or concentration needed to produce a given drug effect.
The distribution of effective doses across a population.
The change in drug response per unit change in dose.
A harmful unintended response to a drug at therapeutic doses.
Total drug exposure of the body to a drug over time.
Harmful effects from excessive drug accumulation in the body.
The length of time a drug produces a therapeutic response.
The dose lethal to half of a tested population.
The gap between effective and toxic drug doses.
The lowest drug level that produces the desired therapeutic effect.
The time needed after dosing for a therapeutic response to begin.
The time required for a drug to produce its maximum therapeutic response.
A mild predictable secondary effect of a drug.
The ratio between toxic and effective drug doses indicating safety.
The dose range that is both safe and effective.
Buildup of a drug in the body when elimination is slower than dosing.
A physiological or psychological need for a drug.
The need for higher drug doses to achieve the same effect.
Ingestion of an excessive amount of a drug causing toxicity.
A physiological need for a drug whose absence causes withdrawal symptoms.
An intense urge to use a drug despite harmful consequences.
The intended beneficial effect produced by a drug.
Symptoms that occur when a dependent drug is stopped.

subjects.name: Major Drug Classes
defs: Blocks conversion of angiotensin I to II, lowering blood pressure and afterload.
Blocks angiotensin II receptors to produce vasodilation and lower blood pressure.
Interferes with clotting factors to prevent formation or extension of blood clots.
Inhibits platelet aggregation to reduce risk of arterial thrombosis.
Blocks beta-adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure.
Inhibits calcium entry into vascular smooth muscle, causing vasodilation and lower pressure.
Increases myocardial contractility and slows heart rate in heart failure.
Powerful diuretic acting on the loop of Henle to remove excess fluid.
Vasodilates coronary vessels to relieve angina and reduce cardiac workload.
Diuretic that excretes sodium while retaining potassium to prevent hypokalemia.
Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase to lower cholesterol and reduce cardiovascular risk.
Promotes sodium and water excretion in the distal tubule to lower blood pressure.
Activates plasminogen to dissolve existing clots in acute events.
Stabilizes neuronal membranes and raises seizure threshold to prevent seizures.
Restores dopamine activity to reduce tremor and rigidity in Parkinson disease.
Antagonizes serotonin and dopamine receptors with fewer extrapyramidal effects.
Enhances GABA activity to produce anxiolysis, sedation, and muscle relaxation.
Increases catecholamine activity to improve alertness and attention.
Inhibits monoamine oxidase to increase neurotransmitter levels in depression.
Modulates neuronal signaling to control mood swings in bipolar disorder.
Agonizes mu opioid receptors to relieve moderate to severe pain.
Inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine for depression and pain.
Selectively inhibits serotonin reuptake to treat depression and anxiety.
Depresses central nervous system activity to induce sleep or calm.
Tricyclic antidepressant blocking reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin.
Blocks dopamine D2 receptors to reduce positive psychotic symptoms.
Bactericidal protein synthesis inhibitor used mainly for gram-negative infections.
Kills or suppresses Plasmodium parasites to treat or prevent malaria.
Suppresses HIV replication through multiple mechanisms to reduce viral load.
Combination therapy targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis to cure infection.
Inhibits fungal ergosterol synthesis, disrupting the cell membrane.
Beta-lactam antibiotic with broader spectrum against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria.
Inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase to block replication.
Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit.
Mimics nucleosides to inhibit viral DNA or RNA polymerase replication.
Beta-lactam inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, causing cell lysis.
Inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis to stop growth of susceptible organisms.
Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit to inhibit bacterial protein synthesis.
Inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis to treat hyperthyroidism in affected clients.
Decreases hepatic glucose production and improves insulin sensitivity.
Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption to treat and prevent osteoporosis.
Reduces inflammation and immune activity for many inflammatory conditions.
Enhances incretin hormones to increase insulin and decrease glucagon.
Mimics incretin to stimulate insulin and slow gastric emptying.
Suppresses ovulation using estrogen and progestin to prevent pregnancy.
Lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular uptake and storage of glucose.
Synthetic thyroid hormone replacing deficient thyroxine in hypothyroidism.
Selectively modulates estrogen receptors in different tissues throughout the body.
Blocks renal glucose reabsorption, promoting urinary glucose excretion.
Stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin and lower glucose.
Reduces pain and fever centrally without significant anti-inflammatory effect.
Neutralizes stomach acid to relieve heartburn and indigestion.
Slows intestinal motility to reduce frequency of loose stools.
Prevents or treats nausea and vomiting by acting on vomiting centers.
Suppresses the cough reflex to relieve nonproductive cough.
Relaxes bronchial smooth muscle to improve airflow in asthma and COPD.
Thins and loosens respiratory secretions to ease productive cough.
Blocks histamine H2 receptors to decrease gastric acid production.
Reduces airway inflammation to control asthma and prevent exacerbations.
Promotes bowel movement to relieve constipation in affected clients.
Inhibits prostaglandin synthesis to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
Irreversibly inhibits gastric proton pump to reduce acid secretion.

subjects.name: Adverse Effects and Drug Interactions
defs: Any harm experienced by a person that results from exposure to a medication.
An undesirable, unexpected, and potentially dangerous response to a drug at therapeutic doses.
An undesired effect of a drug that may occur alongside its intended therapeutic action.
An immune-mediated response that occurs when the body reacts to a drug or substance.
A rare, life-threatening allergic reaction causing breathing difficulty and cardiovascular collapse.
An immune-mediated adverse reaction to a medication that can range from rash to anaphylaxis.
A non-immune adverse reaction where a drug's effects become unacceptable at normal doses.
An exaggerated immune response to a drug that can produce rash, fever, or anaphylaxis.
An unusual, unpredictable drug response often related to individual genetic or metabolic factors.
A drug effect that is opposite to the intended therapeutic effect, such as stimulant-induced drowsiness.
A secondary and usually predictable effect produced by a drug at therapeutic doses.
Combined drug effect equal to the sum of the individual effects of each drug.
An interaction where one drug reduces or blocks the effect of another drug.
A change in a drug's effect caused by concurrent use of another drug.
Increased activity of drug-metabolizing enzymes that lowers concentrations of affected drugs.
Decreased activity of drug-metabolizing enzymes that raises concentrations of affected drugs.
An interaction that changes drug effects at the receptor or target-organ level.
An interaction that alters absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of a drug.
The concurrent use of multiple medications, which increases interaction and adverse-effect risk.
An interaction where one drug enhances the effect of another without having that effect itself.
Combined drug effect that is greater than the sum of each drug's individual effect.
A harmful or amplified effect that occurs when alcohol is combined with a medication.
A condition or factor that makes a particular drug inadvisable or unsafe to use.
A situation where a drug worsens or complicates an existing medical condition.
A change in a drug's effect or absorption caused by food, beverages, or nutrients.
An interaction between a medication and vitamins, minerals, or other dietary components.
The influence of food on drug absorption, which can increase, decrease, or delay it.
Grapefruit juice inhibiting intestinal enzymes and raising levels of certain drugs.
An interaction between herbal supplements and medications that can alter drug effects.
Impaired absorption of nutrients or drugs from the gastrointestinal tract.
A warning to use a drug carefully because of possible risks in certain conditions.
A substance given to counteract the toxic effects of a drug or poison.
A state where the body or mind requires a drug to function normally or avoid withdrawal.
The amount of a drug that can cause death in a given proportion of exposed individuals.
Taking more than the recommended or safe amount of a drug, risking serious harm.
The concentration of a drug measured in blood to guide safe and effective dosing.
The ratio of the toxic dose to the effective dose; higher values indicate safer drugs.
Reduced drug response over time, requiring higher doses to achieve the same effect.
The amount of a drug that produces harmful or poisonous effects in the body.
Harmful effects from excessive drug levels, often when metabolism or excretion is impaired.
Symptoms that occur when a regularly used drug is reduced or stopped abruptly.
Submitting suspected harmful drug reactions to regulatory agencies for safety monitoring.
The FDA's strongest safety warning highlighting serious or life-threatening drug risks.
A manufacturer or regulator action to remove a defective or unsafe drug from the market.
The FDA database that collects adverse event and medication error reports.
The FDA program for reporting adverse events and product problems involving medications.
Any preventable event that may cause inappropriate medication use or patient harm.
FDA-required patient information highlighting serious risks and safe use of specific drugs.
The process of verifying and updating a patient's accurate medication list across care transitions.
The science and activities of detecting, assessing, and preventing adverse drug effects.
Ongoing monitoring of drug safety after a medication has been approved for use.
A risk evaluation and mitigation strategy required to ensure safe use of certain drugs.

subjects.name: Special Populations
defs: Small body mass in children increases drug concentration and sensitivity to effects.
A measure used to calculate drug doses based on a child's body size.
Infants and children have underdeveloped livers, slowing drug metabolism and risking toxicity.
Underdeveloped kidneys in young patients reduce drug clearance and prolong drug effects.
A list identifying drugs that may be harmful or inappropriate for pediatric patients.
Most drug data come from adults, leaving pediatric safety and dosing less studied.
Use of drugs in children without pediatric-specific FDA-approved labeling or dosing.
Ethical and consent challenges limit drug research in infants and children.
Dosing calculated by milligrams per kilogram of body weight or body surface area.
Double-check calculations and use the smallest syringe for precise pediatric doses.
Drug dose determined by multiplying milligrams per kilogram by body weight.
Older adults experience adverse drug reactions more frequently than younger adults.
Aging alters drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion processes.
Altered drug absorption in older adults
Slower gut transit and lower gastric acidity change oral drug absorption.
A list of potentially inappropriate medications for use in older adults.
Reduced liver function in older adults slows drug metabolism and prolongs effects.
Reduced kidney function in older adults slows drug excretion and raises toxicity.
Reviewing all medications to identify interactions, duplications, and needed changes.
Small dose changes in older adults can cause toxicity or subtherapeutic effects.
Concurrent use of multiple medications, increasing interaction and adverse effect risk.
A drug whose risks in older adults may outweigh its expected benefits.
The rapid growth of the older adult population increasing healthcare demand.
Assumption that any medication taken during pregnancy can reach the fetus.
Doubled renal blood flow in pregnancy accelerates drug clearance from body.
Passage of drugs into breast milk, potentially exposing the nursing infant.
Lipid-soluble drugs cross the placenta more easily than protein-bound drugs.
Pregnancy alters absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of drugs.
Movement of drugs across the placenta from pregnant client to fetus.
FDA rule replacing pregnancy categories with narrative drug labeling guidance.
Legacy FDA ABCDX classification of fetal risk for drugs during pregnancy.
Weighing maternal and fetal benefits against risks before giving drugs.
A drug known to cause harm to embryonic or fetal development.
A blood test measuring urea nitrogen to assess kidney function.
Dose modifications needed for patients with long-standing kidney disease.
Hemodialysis can remove some drugs, requiring post-dialysis dosing adjustments.
Modifying dose or frequency to prevent toxicity in kidney disease.
Drugs build up when kidneys fail to excrete them, causing toxicity.
Volume of blood filtered by kidneys per minute, indicating renal function.
Drugs that can damage kidney tissue or worsen renal function.
Impaired kidneys clear drugs more slowly, increasing blood drug levels.
Efficiency of kidneys in removing a drug from the bloodstream.
A waste product measured in blood to evaluate renal function.
Acetaminophen requires caution or avoidance in underlying liver disease.
A liver enzyme used to detect hepatic injury or dysfunction.
An enzyme whose elevation may indicate liver cell injury or damage.
Cirrhotic livers metabolize drugs less effectively, prolonging drug effects.
Reduced metabolism lets drugs build up, increasing toxicity risk.
Liver disease decreases first-pass metabolism, raising oral drug bioavailability.
Liver disease slows drug metabolism, increasing systemic drug concentrations.
Drugs that can injure or damage the liver tissue.
AST and ALT elevations indicate hepatic dysfunction or liver damage.
Liver disease alters plasma protein binding, increasing free drug levels.
